issues.legal_issue: Statutory finality of an order does not exclude the constitutional supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 227.
material_facts: The Sessions Judge's order in an appeal under the forest statute was declared final and not open to challenge in any court.
The State challenged the High Court's refusal to consider supervisory relief, while not contesting the conclusion that a statutory revision was unavailable.
issues.conclusion: The statutory finality clause did not prevent the High Court from considering the matter under Article 227. The Court left open whether Section 482 of the Code could be invoked, set aside the High Court's refusal to exercise Article 227 jurisdiction, and directed it to consider the matter under that provision.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory declaration of finality cannot take away the constitutional jurisdiction preserved by Articles 32, 226 and 227. The Court relied on Lila Vati v. State of Bombay and Union of India v. A.V. Narasimhalu for the principle that statutory finality or exclusion of ordinary court jurisdiction does not exclude constitutional writ jurisdiction. It observed that, given the express finality language in Section 59(3) of the Indian Forest Act as amended, invocation of Section 482 of the Code might not be permissible, but that language could not bar Article 227 jurisdiction.

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: The challenged order was made in an appeal provided by a statute.
predicates.reviewed_order_declared_final: The statute declared the challenged appellate order final or not open to challenge in court.
predicates.constitutional_supervisory_challenge: A litigant asked the High Court to examine the challenged order through its constitutional supervisory jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a statutory appellate order is declared final and a litigant seeks constitutional supervision of it, constitutional supervisory review remains available.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot reject a request for supervisory review without properly considering a material statutory presumption that the lower appellate decision overlooked.
material_facts: Goods being transported in a truck were seized after the person accompanying them failed to produce a required permit.
The forest authority ordered confiscation of the truck.

The Sessions Judge held the confiscation order to be without jurisdiction on the basis that there had been no claim that the goods belonged to the State, without addressing the statutory presumption of State ownership.
The State relied on that presumption in seeking further review, but the High Court rejected supervisory intervention without examining the issue on its merits.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in concluding that no case for examination had been made out. It was directed to consider the State's position concerning the statutory presumption, hear both parties, and decide the matter objectively on its merits and in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 69 of the Indian Forest Act provided the statutory presumption concerning State ownership of forest produce. The Court held that the issue whether the presumption applied was material and required examination; the department's reliance on the presumption meant a separate ownership claim was not necessary. The High Court was required to consider the issue under Article 227, even though the order was declared final under Section 59(3).

rule.if: statutory_appeal_proceeding and state_relied_on_ownership_presumption and appellate_decision_ignored_presumption and higher_court_declined_review_without_examining_it

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: The challenged order was made in an appeal provided by a statute.
predicates.state_relied_on_ownership_presumption: The State relied on a statutory presumption of its ownership of the relevant property.
predicates.appellate_decision_ignored_presumption: The appellate decision did not address the statutory ownership presumption when deciding the dispute.
predicates.higher_court_declined_review_without_exa: The High Court declined supervisory intervention without examining the material presumption issue on its merits.

issues.definition: When the State relies on an ownership presumption that the appellate decision overlooked and the High Court declines review without examining it, the High Court must reconsider the merits through constitutional supervision.
